verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “Over the past few days, I've noticed my skin is sore and red” and describes it as “all over my chest, my hands and arms,” and “It's very itchy and dry,” indicating widespread sore, red, itchy skin for the past few days.

Patient says, “It's all over my chest, my hands and arms, especially inside of the elbows.” There is no mention of the backs of the hands; specifying “including backs of hands” adds a location not stated.

The transcript notes “especially inside of the elbows” but does not explicitly state that this is the worst area; the question “Which is the worst area?” is asked but not answered. Claiming it is the worst is an unsupported addition.
Patient describes, “It's very itchy and dry,” clearly supporting that the affected skin is very itchy and dry.
When asked if the areas are weeping, the doctor asks, “Is it weeping? … Weeping?” and the patient responds, “No,” confirming no weeping from the skin lesions.
On being asked about scratch marks, the patient replies, “I mean, it's very itchy to scratch myself. There's no scratch mark,” supporting that no visible scratch marks are reported.
When asked about thickened skin, patient responds, “No. No, I don't think. I don't think so,” supporting no reported skin thickening.

Discussion: “Have you ever used steroids…?” Patient: “Yes, you used it, but it. It's not helping.” Later clarified as over‑the‑counter hydrocortisone: “over the counter Hydrocortisone, does that ring a bell? Yeah. So you're using the hydrocortisone?” indicating it was tried and not helping.

Patient says, “I realized I've tried also antihistamines and didn't work.” Doctor clarifies “like cetrazene? Yeah, yeah, yeah,” confirming over‑the‑counter antihistamines such as cetirizine were tried without benefit.
Patient: “Yes, I have Eczema in the past,” clearly indicating a history of eczema.
Patient states, “I have asthma,” confirming a history of asthma.
Patient reports, “Usually I use a cream called Dipro Base,” indicating use of Diprobase emollient.
Patient: “In the shower. I use something called Dermal.” This supports use of Dermol/Dermal wash‑type product.

Doctor asks about over‑the‑counter hydrocortisone: “over the counter Hydrocortisone, does that ring a bell? Yeah. So you're using the hydrocortisone?” confirming that the patient has used over‑the‑counter hydrocortisone.

On asthma medication, patient says, “the blue inhaler,” and confirms intermittent use: “So you just use it on and off? Yeah, yeah, yeah.” This is consistent with a salbutamol blue inhaler used as needed.
When asked, “Do you have any allergies to any medication at all?” the patient answers, “No, no allergies,” supporting no known drug allergies.
Patient states, “in my family there is hypothyroidism … My mother.” Clarified: “Who has hypothyroidism? … My mother,” confirming maternal hypothyroidism.
Patient: “in my family there is hypothyroidism and migraine. My mother has migraine,” which supports that the patient's mother has migraine.

The doctor states, “it looks like… it is quite widespread, your eczema,” and the patient describes very itchy, sore skin “over the past few days” and says, “I think it's gotten worse.” This supports a widespread, pruritic flare of eczema worse than baseline.

Regarding asthma: “What medications are you using…? … the blue inhaler.” “So you just use it on and off? Yeah, yeah, yeah. … It's only when I have a flare.” This indicates intermittent asthma managed with a blue (salbutamol‑type) inhaler as needed.

Doctor says, “I'm going to. It's called the antihistamine it's called fexofenadine,” but does not specify twice‑daily dosing in the transcript or explicitly say ‘for two weeks’ for this medication. The twice‑daily for two weeks detail is not stated.

Doctor: “you might probably need a bit more stronger one like betno weight… we will try with some Bettner weight first… You have to use it twice a day for the next couple of weeks.” This matches prescribing topical Betnovate fingertip amounts twice daily for about two weeks.

Doctor advises, “You still need to continue on your emollients like the dermal soap and as well as the depravate [Diprobase]. Yeah. So you still need to use those in the interim,” supporting continued Diprobase and Dermol use.

Doctor instructs, “If there's no improvement, you need to get back to us. Or if you have any kind of adverse reaction, like an allergic reaction… you need to get in touch with us. … If things are getting worse in the next two weeks, call us beforehand.” This covers worsening symptoms and adverse reactions; infection is not explicitly mentioned, but earlier return for worsening is advised, so the general part of the statement is supported.

Doctor states, “we are going to send off the prescription to your pharmacy. It looks like Boots on the systems, is that correct? … So I'll send it across to Boots and it will be there for collecting,” matching sending the prescription to Boots for collection.

There is no counseling in the plan about continued use of the blue inhaler; asthma is discussed in history only. The statement “Advise the patient to continue using the blue inhaler as needed” does not appear in the transcript and is a new plan element.
